causalMechanism.primaryVector: Type 2 diabetes produces distal symmetric polyneuropathy through chronic hyperglycemic and dyslipidemic injury to peripheral nerves and their supporting microvasculature, with a length-dependent pattern reflecting the greatest metabolic load on the longest axons. The result is loss of small-fiber and then large-fiber function (pain and temperature, then vibration and proprioception), neuropathic pain, depressed reflexes, and autonomic involvement. causalMechanism.primaryVector: Type 2 diabetes drives hepatic steatosis and its progression through the same insulin-resistance physiology that defines the diabetes. Chronic hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance in adipose tissue increase free fatty-acid flux to the liver while hepatic de novo lipogenesis is upregulated (SREBP-1c and ChREBP activation), and impaired fatty-acid oxidation plus very-low-density lipoprotein export failure cause triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes. Glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity then promote lipotoxic injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and inflammasome activation; adipose-tissue and gut-derived inflammatory signals drive the transition from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, and activation of hepatic stellate cells produces progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Because type 2 diabetes also accelerates fibrosis once steatosis is present, it is one of the strongest risk factors for progression rather than merely a co-traveler. The quantitative evidence is direct and large: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 156 studies and 1,832,125 patients found NAFLD prevalence of 65.04% (95% CI 61.79-68.15) and NASH prevalence of 31.55% in people with type 2 diabetes, with clinically significant fibrosis (F2-F4) in 35.54% and advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) in 14.95% of those with NAFLD; and a prospective cohort of 501 adults with type 2 diabetes systematically assessed by MRI-PDFF and elastography found NAFLD in 65%, advanced fibrosis in 14%, and cirrhosis in 6%, with obesity and insulin use associated with advanced fibrosis. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), fatty liver disease developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim, and the evidence recited above — a majority prevalence of steatosis among people with type 2 diabetes together with a shared causal physiology and a demonstrated progression gradient with diabetes severity — supports the conclusion that steatotic liver disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (duration, control, treatment), the hepatic findings (imaging or biopsy demonstrating steatosis, and staging of fibrosis where available), and the chronology, and address competing causes — alcohol use (which may co-exist and is excluded only by a reliable history), other causes of chronic liver disease (viral hepatitis, autoimmune and drug-induced hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency), medications (corticosteroids, methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and other metabolic contributors (obesity, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism). Rating follows the documented severity under DC 7345/7312 criteria or by analogy under § 4.20; where the pre-existing hepatic disease is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Type 2 diabetes causes gastroparesis through chronic hyperglycemic injury to the autonomic and enteric nervous systems that regulate the stomach. Sustained hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress, advanced glycation end-product accumulation, and microvascular disease in the vagus nerve and gastric myenteric plexus; the resulting vagal neuropathy, loss of interstitial cells of Cajal (the gastric pacemaker cells), and depletion of neuronal nitric oxide synthase impair fundal accommodation and antral contractility and cause pyloric spasm, so gastric contents empty too slowly. The clinical picture is early satiety, prolonged postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and the condition is a complication of long-standing diabetes; it is associated with increased mortality and complicates glycemic control because of unpredictable absorption of food and medication. The epidemiologic evidence is direct: a systematic review and meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of gastroparesis among patients with diabetes to be 9.3%, with the highest subgroup prevalence in type 2 diabetes at 12.5% (95% CI 7.7-17.3), and a large US epidemiological study of 82.6 million patients identified type 2 diabetes as the single most common cause of gastroparesis (51.7% of cases) — ahead of postsurgical effects, medication effects, and idiopathic cases. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), gastroparesis developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim: the diabetes is the proximate cause through diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and no new injury is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (duration, control, complications), the gastric-emptying study (scintigraphy or a validated breath test) or the clinical diagnosis with exclusion of obstruction by endoscopy, the symptom chronology relative to diabetes duration, and treatment response; and exclude competing causes — medication effects (opioids, GLP-1 receptor agonists, anticholinergics), prior gastric or esophageal surgery, hypothyroidism, Parkinson disease and other neurological disease, connective tissue disease, amyloidosis, and viral injury. Where pre-existing gastroparesis is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. Because gastric dysmotility in diabetes is evaluated under DC 7356, the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Type 2 diabetes causes diabetic nephropathy through chronic hyperglycemic injury to the glomerulus. Hyperglycemia drives glomerular hyperfiltration and intraglomerular hypertension, non-enzymatic glycation of proteins, and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and of pro-fibrotic growth factors; the resulting mesangial matrix expansion, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and podocyte injury progressively impair the filtration barrier, which appears clinically first as microalbuminuria and then as macroalbuminuria with declining glomerular filtration rate. Hypertension and smoking accelerate the same process, and glycemic control slows it — the therapeutic prediction that anchors the causal direction. The evidence is direct and interventional: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies across 13 countries found a pooled prevalence of chronic kidney disease among type 2 diabetes patients of 27% (95% CI 21-33%), identifying diabetes as the leading cause of chronic kidney disease; the UK Prospective Diabetes Study randomized trial (3,867 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients followed for 10 years) found that intensive blood-glucose control produced a 25% risk reduction (95% CI 7-40, p = 0.0099) in microvascular endpoints, including the renal manifestations of diabetes; and a longitudinal cohort of 694 type 2 diabetes patients followed 4.5 years documented the natural history — 36.6% with microalbuminuria and 2.4% with macroalbuminuria at baseline, 9.9% progressing albuminuria stage, and 32.5% deteriorating in renal function. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), diabetic nephropathy developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (onset, duration, control with glycated hemoglobin history), the renal findings (serial urine albumin-creatinine ratios and estimated glomerular filtration rates with dates, and renal imaging where performed), and the chronology of albuminuria relative to diabetes duration; and address competing causes — hypertensive nephrosclerosis (which commonly coexists and is rated under § 4.115 principles regarding the close interrelationships of cardiovascular and renal disability), glomerulonephritis, toxic nephropathy from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or other agents (DC 7535), interstitial and gouty nephropathy (DC 7537), multiple myeloma and amyloidosis, and viral nephropathies (DC 7544). Because the schedule has a dedicated code for renal involvement in diabetes, the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

The combination converts a normal anatomic narrowing into a focal compressive mononeuropathy producing burning pain, numbness, and paresthesias along the medial ankle and plantar surface, with a positive Tinel sign and electrodiagnostic slowing across the tunnel. Rinkel et al. (PMID 30113445), a cross-sectional study in both diabetic and nondiabetic subjects, reported a prevalence of tibial nerve entrapment at the tarsal tunnel of 44.9 percent in diabetic patients versus 26.5 percent in nondiabetic subjects, and assessed the validity of the Tinel sign for the diagnosis. Rinkel et al. (PMID 32276769) then followed the natural history of tarsal tunnel syndrome in diabetic subjects and reported that tibial nerve entrapment is highly prevalent in diabetes, producing significantly more neuropathic complaints and concomitant sensory disturbance, and they studied its relationship to incident diabetic foot ulceration. Omirah et al. (PMID 40591366) examined the association between body mass index, HbA1c level and tarsal tunnel syndrome severity in a clinical and neurophysiological study, treating the condition as a focal compressive entrapment neuropathy of the posterior tibial nerve in which obesity and diabetes are systemic risk factors. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected diabetes is asserted to have produced a distinct focal entrapment mononeuropathy with its own diagnostic code, not merely a diffuse distal polyneuropathy. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing tarsal tunnel syndrome (for example, from prior ankle fracture, hindfoot deformity, or a space-occupying lesion) and the claim is that the diabetic metabolic and structural changes measurably worsened a baseline entrapment, in which case the diabetic increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing compression and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a documented diagnosis of type 2 diabetes with its laboratory confirmation and duration; clinical localization of symptoms to the tarsal tunnel; and electrodiagnostic confirmation — nerve conduction studies showing focal slowing or conduction block of the tibial nerve across the tarsal tunnel, ideally with comparison of plantar sensory responses with the unaffected side — rather than reliance on a Tinel sign alone, since the physical sign alone had imperfect validity in the cited study.
